exercise.title: Why does an infinite polynomial need a domain?

statement.p: A finite polynomial such as 1+x+x^2+x^3 is defined for every real x. The infinite expression 1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots is not. In your own words, why does a power series become a numerical series at each input, and why can the same formula converge at one x and diverge at another?

hint.p: There is no last term to add. At each fixed x, you must ask whether the partial sums settle. Geometric series already show that the answer depends on the size of x.

exercise.title: Why does a power series have a center?

statement.p: A power series centered at a is built from powers of x-a. In your own words, why is the center always a point of convergence, and why is distance from that center the quantity that controls the rest of the story?

hint.p: At x=a, every term after the constant is zero, so there is nothing infinite left to add. Farther from the center, the powers (x-a)^n grow or shrink according to |x-a|.

subsection.title: Radius and interval of convergence
subsection.p: The examples suggest a pattern. A power series converges in a symmetric region around its center. The endpoints need separate attention.

This explains the shape: once a power series converges at one point, it converges at all points closer to the center.

The opposite statement follows by the same logic. If the series diverges at some point, it must diverge at every point farther from the center. Otherwise convergence farther out would force convergence closer in.
That is why the convergence set is an interval centered at a, with possible choices about the two endpoints.

exercise.title: Why is the convergence set always an interval?

statement.p: A power series converges in a disk of some radius R around its center, with endpoints left to be tested. In your own words, why can the set of convergent inputs not be a scattered collection of points, and what do the three possibilities R=0, R=\infty, and 0<R<\infty mean?

hint.p: If the series converges at some point, it converges absolutely at every closer point. That forces a solid interval around the center, possibly degenerating to a single point or expanding to the whole line.

subsection.title: Endpoint testing
subsection.p: The radius tells us what happens inside and outside. It does not tell us what happens at the endpoints.
The reason is simple: the Ratio Test often gives the limiting value 1 at the endpoints, and the Ratio Test is silent when the limit is 1.

exercise.title: Why must endpoints be tested separately?

statement.p: The radius decides the open interval of guaranteed absolute convergence. The two endpoints are another story. In your own words, why can two series share a radius but have different intervals of convergence, and what extra work do the endpoints require?

hint.p: At an endpoint the geometric safety margin disappears, and you are back to a numerical series. That series may converge, diverge, or converge only conditionally, independently of the interior.
